t: How To Transform A Difficult Class
q: The most common approach to an especially difficult class is to lower the bar.
It’s natural human tendency to choose the easier road when given the chance. Unless challenged, few students in a difficult class (or school) will hold themself to a higher standard.

When your actions prove that you don’t believe they’re capable of more or better, both academically and behaviorally, they accept it as truth. They predictably fulfill the prophecy you set for them , thus giving you exactly what you expect.
And far from meeting you halfway, your students will push and push until there are no more consequences for any misbehavior. Invertebrate teachers get crushed in challenging environments.

So what should you do? The opposite. You raise the bar, higher than they’ve ever experienced. You become a stickler for the little things to show your students that they do matter and that they are worth it.
Challenge your students every minute of the day. Be worthy of their respect. Love them, provide great instruction, and offer them a new and hopeful prophecy to fulfill.
x: Lowering standards for a difficult class is a virtual guarantee that behavior worsens rather than improves.

t: “I’m Already Stressing About Next Year. What Can I Do?”
q: I'd like to speak a bit into any anxiety you might be feeling right now about your adequacy for meeting the challenges ahead.

Here's my point: gaps (differences in preparation) are part of the job. Always have been. It won't make any headlines, but here's my prediction: 21-22 will only be an exaggerated version of this familiar challenge.
Learning is not the same thing as uploading files into the cloud; it's a partnership. Create all the standards you want, but you'll never fully standardize it.

I mean, c'mon — the world may have changed, but human beings are not different creatures than they were two autumns ago. We're still all souls comprised of thoughts, emotions, beliefs, bodies, and relationships.
Though gaps exist, the fundamentals don't change. And it's those fundamentals — the arts and sciences of the head and the heart — that hold the keys to remedying gaps in preparation.
It won't be a lazy person's work, for sure. Never is. Pack your hard hat and your work boots because you and I will be called upon to master the fundamentals in ways we've not been before.

t: How To Build Rapport When You Have A Quiet Personality
q: It’s easy to admire teachers with the gift of gab, high social IQ, and ability to build rapport so quickly.
With the right approach, you never have to do anything or be anything you’re not in order to build strong, influential rapport with your students.
The highest level of rapport between you and your students happens when they come to you . It’s when they’re drawn to you.

If you’re a regular reader of SCM, then you know it’s to simply be consistently pleasant. Be good natured in all your dealings with students, especially when in front of the entire class, and rapport develops organically.
You just have to be pleasant and they’ll come to you. And when they come to you, conversation is natural and effortless.
The Law of Reciprocity is so strong and predictable that although you may not know some of your students well, at least on a personal, non-academic level, they’ll feel like they know you.
x: Linsin reassures introverted teachers that building rapport requires no verbal gift or outgoing personality.
Proactively trying to draw out shy or quiet students can make many of them uncomfortable rather than building genuine rapport.
The strongest rapport forms when students come to the teacher voluntarily rather than the teacher pursuing conversation.
Being consistently pleasant in every interaction, especially in front of the whole class, is the one method that works for any personality type.

The Law of Reciprocity means students feel connected to a consistently kind teacher even without frequent personal conversation.

t: How To Protect Black Students From Teacher Racial Discrimination https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2020/07/04/black-students-teacher-racial-discrimination/
q: Studies show that Black students are disciplined more severely than their White classmates for the same misbehavior.
Our approach protects Black students from being singled out, profiled, and punished more harshly because of the color of their skin.
Consequences are enforced by the teacher like a good referee calls a foul in a sports game. That is, a student is informed that they broke a rule unemotionally and with respect.
Teachers consistently enforce consequences whenever a rule is broken. Consistent means every single time regardless of who breaks a rule .

Behavior contracts, which are often directed at Black children, are forbidden. They’re a form of labeling that tell students (and their classmates) very clearly that they’re different, less than, and not good enough.
With SCM, any existing or future racial discrimination or classroom management bias becomes glaringly obvious to all stakeholders and nearly impossible to hide.

t: How To Be A Role Model For Your Students (And Not An Internet Troll)
q: If you say you’re going to follow through on your classroom management plan and you don’t do it, then your students won’t trust you.
Consistency in word and deed is rare, but it will make you stick out like a flower among thorns.
It’s not about your politics. It’s not about your wants and needs. It’s not about the difficulties in your life, your future goals, or your stressful morning. Be a pro and keep them to yourself.
They notice how you treat others. They notice if you play favorites and the subtle way in which you smile at some but not others.
There are so few role models in this day and age that students will bend over backward to be around and please the real thing.
x: Consistently following through on the classroom management plan is what earns a teacher students' trust; failing to do so erodes it.
Linsin lays out eight behaviors that make a teacher into a genuine role model rather than a source of negativity students quietly mimic.

q: This post isn’t meant to be humorous. It isn’t meant to be judgemental or hypercritical or make you feel like a failure.
You see, viewing classroom management through a negative lens—as in, what not to do —can bring the greatest clarity.
Wincing as we recognize ourselves in the list below can help us identify those areas holding us back from having the well-behaved class we really want.
Indeed, you may have questions about some of the items on the list and why they’re a bad thing. Rest assured, all have been written about extensively on this website.

t: Finish Like We’d Like to Start: The Return of These 6 Things
q: I was talking with my friend Dr. T a couple weeks back, and he said this line that had immediate resonance: “We're just trying to finish the year like we'd like to start.” That's just right.
The whole idea behind These 6 Things is that human beings can't become experts at everything. I'd like to, but I can't. I'm finite. So are you.

Instead, the idea is that as a professional you aim at mastering the use of these six elements. Your goal at all times is to simplify your planning and instruction — you want just the fundamental work that produces student growth.
You push in one to two areas per year and maintain the rest. I describe this thinking in the book's conclusion. It's really important.

This actually isn't as time-consuming as it sounds because I'm going to use the same exact intervention for every child, and all but one intervention will be administered with the entire class simultaneously.
First, taking the time to write this out has given me a boost of motivation. It's bolstered my beliefs in the final weeks of school.
Third, I want leaders and teachers to get a sense for how new isn't better by default. I do need to bring some nuance to what I just said, but I've not the time today so I'll end by saying this.

t: I’m In. Here’s the (Start of the) Plan.
q: There was just one problem: I'd have to be done teaching and writing. After all, I'm not willing to work around the clock and sacrifice my family for success.
There is just something about this job — remote or in-person, masked or not, grading or teaching, connecting or troubleshooting — that feels like home.

No. It's just that I still think teaching is good. I think learning is beautiful. I think schools are still the places with the greatest potential for advancing the long-term flourishing of each child.

The system we aim to improve isn't policies and procedures — it's people. It's not what's said a few times during a single day of PD — it's what's said a thousand times in the hearts and minds and mouths of the folks who work within the system.
Changing things on paper without changing things in the hearts and minds of teachers doesn't do much. Lip service is an illusion; it only deepens our dysphoria.
None of what I just said is easy. But it's reality. There are no better partners than reality.
